brave.title: CEDAR PARK ASSEMBLY OF GOD OF KIRKLAND, WASHINGTON V. KUDERER, No. 23-35560 (9th Cir. 2026) :: Justia
brave.snippet:
A church in Washington State challenged the validity of two state laws: the Reproductive Parity Act, which requires health insurance carriers to include coverage for all federally approved contraceptives and, if maternity care is covered, for abortions; and a longstanding conscience statute, which allows employers to object to purchasing coverage for specific healthcare services on religious or moral grounds.
The United States District Court for the Western District of Washington found that the church had standing to sue, but granted summary judgment in favor of the state defendants on the merits, concluding that the challenged laws did not violate the Free Exercise Clause or church autonomy doctrine. Both sides appealed. Previously, the Ninth Circuit vacated the district court’s judgment for lack of standing, but after the Supreme Court’s decision in Diamond Alternative Energy, LLC v.
EPA, 606 U.S. 100 (2025), it vacated its own opinion and reheard the case. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit held that the church had Article III standing, as the laws caused it to facilitate abortion indirectly. Assuming, without deciding, that the laws burdened the church’s religious exercise, the court concluded that the laws are neutral and generally applicable.

# CEDAR PARK ASSEMBLY OF GOD OF KIRKLAND WASHINGTON v. PATTY KUDERER BOB FERGUSON (2026)
## United States Court of Appeals, Ninth Circuit.
###
CEDAR PARK ASSEMBLY OF GOD OF KIRKLAND, WASHINGTON, Plaintiff-Appellant / Cross-Appellee, v. PATTY KUDERER, in her official capacity as Insurance Commissioner for the State of Washington; BOB FERGUSON, in his official capacity as Governor of the State of Washington, Defendants-Appellees/Cross-Appellants.
### No. 23-35560, No. 23-35585
### Decided: September 14, 2026
### Before: Susan P. Graber, Consuelo M. Callahan, and Lucy H. Koh, Circuit Judges.

Plaintiff Cedar Park Assembly of God of Kirkland, Washington, is a church that objects, on religious grounds, to abortion and to some forms of contraception. As an employer, Plaintiff purchases for its employees group health insurance that covers comprehensive maternity care. Plaintiff challenges the validity of the Reproductive Parity Act of 2018 (the “Parity Act”), a Washington statute that regulates health insurance carriers. The Parity Act requires carriers to include, in the health plans that they offer, coverage for all federally approved contraceptives and, if the health plan covers maternity care, for abortions. Plaintiff also challenges Washington's thirty-year-old conscience statute, which shields an employer that buys health insurance from any requirement to purchase coverage for a health care service to which the employer objects on either religious or moral grounds. Plaintiff alleges that those laws, taken together, violate the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment and Plaintiff's right to religious autonomy to the extent that they require Plaintiff to provide coverage for, pay for, or facilitate access to abortion and certain contraceptives, either directly or indirectly.

The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled Monday that Washington can keep requiring health plans covering maternity care to also cover abortion, ending, for now, a six-year constitutional challenge brought by Cedar Park Assembly of God in Kirkland.

At issue are two state laws. The Reproductive Parity Act of 2018, better known as Senate Bill 6219, requires insurance carriers to include abortion coverage in any health plan that covers maternity care. Washington’s three-decade-old conscience statute lets an employer refuse to purchase coverage for a service it objects to on religious or moral grounds, while requiring the employee’s carrier to separately tell workers how to obtain the excluded service anyway. Cedar Park, which insures roughly 140 people and teaches that abortion is sinful, argued that combination leaves it facilitating abortion no matter what it does.

The panel disagreed. It also did something the state spent years trying to prevent.

Cedar Park Assembly of God in Kirkland employs about 140 people and holds to the same pro-life position as every Assemblies of God church in the country.

A church in Washington State challenged the validity of two state laws: the Reproductive Parity Act, which requires health insurance carriers to include coverage for all federally approved contraceptives and, if maternity care is covered, for abortions; and a longstanding conscience statute, which allows employers to object to purchasing coverage for specific healthcare services on religious or moral grounds.
The United States District Court for the Western District of Washington found that the church had standing to sue, but granted summary judgment in favor of the state defendants on the merits, concluding that the challenged laws did not violate the Free Exercise Clause or church autonomy doctrine. EPA, 606 U.S. 100 (2025), it vacated its own opinion and reheard the case. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit held that the church had Article III standing, as the laws caused it to facilitate abortion indirectly. Assuming, without deciding, that the laws burdened the church’s religious exercise, the court concluded that the laws are neutral and generally applicable.
